payload.throughline: Choose a sociological lens by identifying the unit of analysis and the mechanism the case asks you to explain.

learner_content_blocks: Low-stakes starting check: identify which part of a brief case carries the explanatory work. This check does not select a route or award exit credit.

You will compare two lenses about meaning. Symbolic interactionism explains how people interpret symbols and negotiate meanings in interaction; social constructionism explains how shared definitions and categories are collectively produced and maintained.

Use two questions. First, where is the action: in an encounter among people, or across shared practices and institutions? Second, what changes: an interpretation used during interaction, or a category treated as socially real?

An encounter-level cue supports symbolic interactionism when people act from meanings they interpret and revise. A category-maintenance cue supports social constructionism when coordinated language, records, rules, or routines stabilize a shared definition.

Picture two zoom settings. The interaction zoom follows symbol → interpretation → response → revised meaning. The construction zoom follows shared definition → repeated practice → institutional reinforcement → taken-for-granted category.

I do not choose from the topic alone. If coworkers change what a badge means through repeated exchanges, I choose symbolic interactionism. If a committee, forms, and policies make a new worker category durable, I choose social constructionism. Cost-benefit language would point elsewhere.

A campus calls certain rooms quiet zones. In one case, students learn that a raised finger means “lower your voice” through repeated encounters. The decisive mechanism is interpretation of a symbol during interaction, so the interaction lens fits.

In a second case, maps, reservation software, signs, and conduct rules collectively establish what counts as a quiet zone. The decisive mechanism is stabilization of a shared category, so the construction lens fits.
With support, underline the unit of analysis, then name whether the case turns on negotiated interpretation or collective category maintenance.
With less support, use the cue pair encounter/interpretation versus shared-practice/category.
Choose the better meaning lens on a fresh case without an answer-bearing cue.

Boundary: a social setting alone does not make either meaning lens correct. If the case asks how one actor selects an option by expected costs and benefits, a rational-choice lens—not either meaning lens—does the explanatory work.
Near-use exit: select the meaning lens for a fresh encounter in which a symbol acquires a shared interpretation.
Changed-task exit: select the meaning lens for a category stabilized across organizational rules and records.
Repair the near-use function: name the participants, the symbol, the interpreted meaning, and the response. Choose symbolic interactionism only when that interaction chain explains the outcome.
Fresh re-entry: apply the encounter-level selection rule to a new symbol and new participants. The prior item’s wording and answer are not reused.
Repair the changed-task function: list the category and the repeated collective practices that make it durable. Choose social constructionism only when those practices explain the outcome.
Fresh re-entry: apply the category-maintenance selection rule to a new institution and a new shared definition.
Recap: choose by mechanism, not topic. Negotiated interpretation in encounters points to symbolic interactionism; collective stabilization of shared categories points to social constructionism.
Low-stakes starting check: decide whether a case is about one actor choosing from a menu or partners maintaining an exchange relationship. This check does not select a route or award exit credit.

You will compare exchange and rational-choice lenses. Rational choice foregrounds one actor selecting an option under expected costs, benefits, and constraints. Exchange theory foregrounds an ongoing relationship of reciprocal rewards, costs, dependence, and alternatives.
Use the unit first. One actor plus alternatives points toward rational choice. Two or more interdependent partners plus repeated give-and-receive points toward exchange theory.
For exchange power, compare dependence. A partner who needs the relationship less or has better alternatives can usually demand more favorable terms.
Use two ledgers. The choice ledger belongs to one actor and compares options. The relationship ledger spans partners and tracks reciprocal rewards, costs, dependence, and outside alternatives.

If a commuter compares price, travel time, and reliability before buying a pass, I use rational choice. If two coworkers keep trading schedule coverage and one has better alternatives, I use exchange theory and examine dependence.
A student selects one of three study locations by expected quiet, travel time, and price. One actor is comparing alternatives, so rational choice fits.
Two lab partners repeatedly trade equipment access and data analysis. One partner has many alternative collaborators, so that less-dependent partner holds more exchange power.
With support, name the unit—actor or relationship—then identify payoff comparison or reciprocal dependence.
With less support, use the cue pair option menu versus relationship ledger.
Select the better exchange lens in a fresh case without an answer-bearing hint.

Boundary: unequal outcomes alone do not prove exchange theory. The case must connect inequality to dependence, reciprocal resources, or alternatives. Meaning negotiated through symbols belongs to a different lens.
Near-use exit: identify the lens for an ongoing reciprocal relationship and predict its continuation.
Changed-task exit: identify the lens for one actor choosing a standalone alternative from expected payoffs.
Repair the near-use function: name each partner, what each gives and receives, and which alternatives make each partner more or less dependent.
Fresh re-entry: apply the relationship-ledger rule to new partners and new exchanged resources.
Repair the changed-task function: name one actor, list the alternatives, and compare expected benefits, costs, and constraints without inventing a relationship.
Fresh re-entry: apply the one-actor choice rule to a new decision and new payoff dimensions.
Recap: rational choice uses one actor’s option ledger; exchange theory uses a relationship ledger. In exchange, better alternatives reduce dependence and increase bargaining power.

question_evidence_plan.changed_dimension_detail: Changes from interpreting a symbol in a recurring encounter to identifying institutional practices that stabilize a category.
Uses municipal maps, codes, and plans rather than university records while preserving the category-stabilization decision.
Changes from explaining relationship persistence to selecting a lens for one actor’s constrained option comparison.
Uses a healthcare scheduling choice instead of a data-storage choice while preserving the one-actor payoff comparison.
